title: Show your work
lede: Chi-Chi’s was a subsidiary for its last sixteen years, so the primary sources are the SEC filings of its owners and of the company that bought its real estate, and the CDC’s two reports on the outbreak. Its years as a public company, 1977 to 1988, predate EDGAR; for those we rely on the chain’s own history page and a reference history, and say so.

notes.label: Derived
notes.text: Sales fell 33% from 1996 to 2002: 1 − $186.4M ÷ $278.1M.[^4][^7] $450M of notes is $300.0M of senior notes plus $150.0M principal of discount notes; the discount notes raised $109.0M.[^46] $173M + $62M + $35M = $270M, which matches Family Restaurants’ stated price of about $270.0M; the pairing of the two filings is ours.[^11][^46] 2002 divisional EBITDA of $9,161,000 is 4.9% of sales of $186,400,000.[^7] The waffle shares are 23 ÷ 76 and 15 ÷ 76, and $42.5M ÷ 76 ≈ $559,000.[^18] 35 + 25 + 15 + 1 = 76.[^19] 9,000 ÷ 601 ≈ 15.0.[^12][^13] 4,931 × $162.23 = $799,956.[^23] Twenty-six days is October 8 to November 3, 2003.[^9][^25] “Six of the seven years” counts the comparable-sales figures for 1996 to 2002.[^4][^5][^7] That Chi-Chi’s was Prandium’s largest chain after 2000 is from its 2001 sales of $205.9M out of $289.9M.[^6] The timeline’s “fifty years” is 1975–76 to 2025.

notes.label: The homepage sparkline
notes.text: The card’s series (1, 92, 200, 235, 202, 177, 153, 136, 76, 0, 1) mixes kinds of count: the company’s own figure for year five[^1], a reference history’s 200 for 1986[^2], 235 operated or franchised in January 1994[^3], company-operated plus franchised and licensed at the end of 1996, 1998, 2000 and 2002[^4][^5][^7], the 76 properties in the Outback sale, which is a transaction and not a census of open restaurants[^18], zero after the closing[^21] and the one licensed restaurant open since 2025.[^36]

notes.label: Conflicts between sources
notes.text: **The founding year.** A reference history and the revived company say 1975; the chain’s own history page said the original restaurant was created in 1976, a local-history site says it opened in 1976, a 2025 local report says the founder started it in 1976, and the closing message thanked customers “of the past 27 years,” which counts from 1977.[^1][^2][^22][^37][^38][^42] We head the page 1975 and say so here. **The place.** The company’s page calls it a Minneapolis bar “now known as the Richfield Chi-Chi’s”; the reference history says “downtown.”[^1][^2] **The name.** The company said it was the nickname of McDermott’s wife. A local-history site reports that McDermott told the Minneapolis Star in 1977 it was Spanish slang; we did not read that article, so that is **unverified**.[^1][^42] **The outbreak.** The CDC’s first report gives about 555 cases and three deaths as of November 20, 2003, and its final study 601 patients and three deaths. Press reports from 2004 onward give 660 ill and four dead; we could not find the basis for the higher figures and use the CDC’s.[^12][^13][^20][^23] **Restaurants in late 2003.** 128 in 20 states in a wire report of the filing; “all its 100 locations” in the AP a month later; and plans to close 11 more in a business journal.[^14][^16][^17] **The 1988 sale.** $235M in two secondary sources; we did not find a contemporary report or filing. The reference history gives 129 company-operated and 77 franchised restaurants at the sale, and a newspaper “more than 230” at the peak.[^2][^15] **The 1994 deal.** Family Restaurants says Foodmaker received $205.0M in cash less assumed leases and debt; Foodmaker says $208M less about $35M of debt, or about $173M. Family Restaurants says Chi-Chi’s operated or franchised 235 restaurants; the reference history says 237. A newspaper dates the deal to 1993, when it was agreed.[^2][^3][^11][^15] **Profits in the 1980s.** The reference history gives peak 1984 net income as $16.7M in one paragraph and $15.6M in another.[^2] **Hormel.** A magazine says Hormel “bought the rights” to the brand in the United States in 1987; Hormel’s own filings list the trademark among those “owned or licensed.”[^27][^41]

notes.label: Secondary and retrospective
notes.text: Everything before 1994 rests on the chain’s own history page and a reference history, not on filings: first-year sales, the 92 restaurants, 1980s profits, Hal Smith’s changes, the Foodmaker price and the 1990 and 1992 sales figures.[^1][^2] The Courier-Journal, Tribune-Review and 2004 Associated Press articles were read as reproduced on a plaintiffs’ law firm’s websites, not on the newspapers’ own.[^15][^20][^23] The date of Pennsylvania’s advisory comes from a 2020 television retrospective.[^25] The status of restaurants in Belgium and Vienna comes from one magazine article and is **unverified**.[^41] Jack Butorac’s statement that Foodmaker lost 55 percent of sales in two years is his own and is contradicted in direction, if not in detail, by the reference history, which has sales rising to 1990.[^2][^15]

notes.label: Unknown
notes.text: Chi-Chi’s own profit or loss for any year after 1988. Division sales for 1994 and 1995. How many restaurants were open on the last day. What creditors of Chi-Chi’s, Inc. recovered and when the case closed. Whether Chi-Chi’s recovered anything from its suppliers. What became of the buyer’s October 2003 letter of intent, beyond the fact that no sale closed. How and when the restaurant trademarks passed to Hormel. The terms of the 2024 licence. Whether any Chi-Chi’s restaurant operates outside the United States today.

notes.label: How we read the sources
notes.text: SEC filings were downloaded from EDGAR as full-text submissions and searched; the figures in the charts were read from the “Selected Operating Data” tables.[^4][^5][^6][^7] The CDC report would not load from cdc.gov and was read in an Internet Archive copy.[^12] The New England Journal of Medicine study was read as its abstract only, retrieved through the National Library of Medicine’s interface; the PubMed page itself did not load for us.[^13] The chain’s own pages were read in Internet Archive captures.[^1][^22][^45] Newspaper and trade articles were loaded directly and read in full, except that the NBC News page showed only its opening paragraph and a photo caption.[^24] We could not load the Star Tribune, The New York Times or the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, and cite none of them. The two live websites were read on October 8, 2026.[^28][^38]

notes.label: Images
notes.text: Three photographs are from Wikimedia Commons under the licences stated.[^43] The building in the third is identified as a former Chi-Chi’s only by its photographer’s title. Website images are cropped from Internet Archive captures.[^1][^22][^45] We did not use the chain’s logo, and the drawings avoid it. Embedded commercials are shown as they aired and include it. The accent red was matched by eye to the signs in the 2011 photograph.

notes.label: General knowledge
notes.text: That Jack in the Box is a fast-food chain and that Taco Bell is a Mexican-style fast-food chain. That Monaca is in Beaver County, north-west of Pittsburgh (also stated in several sources above).
